meta.name: CHF Exacerbation — Mild Pulmonary Edema, CPAP Response

patient.name: Walter Ostrowski
patient.chiefComplaint: Increasing shortness of breath and leg swelling

history.hpi: Wife reports three days of gradually worsening shortness of breath and bilateral leg swelling, with the patient sleeping upright in his recliner the past two nights because he can't breathe lying flat. Tonight his breathing suddenly worsened after dinner, becoming labored and audibly wet-sounding, prompting the 911 call.
history.lastOralIntake: Dinner (ham and canned soup) approximately 2 hours prior to onset
history.events: Wife called 911 after patient became acutely more short of breath sitting in his recliner after a high-sodium dinner

scene.location: Single-story home, living room, patient seated upright in a recliner
scene.bystanders: Wife present, called 911, reports 3 days of worsening symptoms
visualCues: Patient sitting bolt upright in recliner, leaning slightly forward
Visible use of accessory muscles, labored breathing
Bilateral lower extremity swelling visible above the sock line
Multiple pillows stacked on the bed visible through the bedroom doorway
Home oxygen concentrator present but not in use

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 71-year-old male with a history of CHF sitting upright in a recliner in visible respiratory distress, with audible wet breath sounds and bilateral pedal edema.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Labored, use of accessory muscles, bibasilar rales audible without stethoscope
otherFindings: Bibasilar rales to mid-lung fields on auscultation
Sitting in tripod-like posture, unable to tolerate lying flat

transitions.condition: Crew recognizes severe respiratory distress from pulmonary edema and escalates therapy to CPAP, coaching the patient through mask placement.

phases.name: CPAP initiated and coached
phases.description: Crew escalates oxygen therapy to CPAP for severe respiratory distress from suspected pulmonary edema, coaching the patient through mask placement and titrating to target oxygenation.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing signs of pulmonary edema with worsening hypoxia despite supplemental oxygen, the crew escalates to CPAP per the escalating-therapy approach in the Respiratory Distress guideline, coaching the patient through the unfamiliar sensation of positive pressure.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, CPAP mask in place with good seal
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improving, still using accessory muscles but less pronounced, RR decreasing
otherFindings: CPAP mask coached into place with adequate seal
Bibasilar rales persist but less pronounced
Patient tolerating mask after initial coaching
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Nods and gives thumbs up between breaths, mask in place

expectedActions.shortAction: Escalate therapy from supplemental O2 to CPAP for severe respiratory distress
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) should be administered for severe respiratory distress via BVM, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP)
expectedActions.rationale: CPAP recruits alveoli and reduces preload, directly addressing pulmonary edema physiology.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

expectedActions.shortAction: Titrate oxygen/CPAP settings to target SpO2 94-98%
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Give supplemental oxygen for dyspnea to a target of 94–98% saturation. Escalate from a nasal cannula as needed to reach this goal
expectedActions.rationale: Avoids both hypoxia and unnecessary over-oxygenation.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

expectedActions.shortAction: Coach and reassure patient through CPAP mask placement to achieve tolerance
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: The key to successful use of NIV in a patient who has not used it before is coaching and explanation of the process and reassurance of the patient
expectedActions.rationale: First-time CPAP patients often resist the mask without verbal coaching, delaying effective therapy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Place waveform capnography in-line with CPAP to monitor ventilatory status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Should be used in spontaneously breathing patients who are: on NIV
expectedActions.rationale: Continuous capnography helps detect early deterioration on NIV before pulse oximetry changes.

expectedActions.shortAction: Maintain continuous, uninterrupted CPAP mask seal through transport to ED bedside
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Once initiated and patient is tolerating mask, DO NOT discontinue CPAP/BiPAP until patient is on the emergency department stretcher and hospital CPAP/BiPAP is immediately available for patient to be switched over, or physician is at bedside and requesting CPAP/BiPAP be discontinued. Breaking the mask seal causes a significant decrease in airway pressures and may lead to abrupt decompensation due to atelectasis and alveolar collapse.
expectedActions.rationale: Breaking the seal at any point rapidly reverses the therapeutic PEEP effect, risking sudden decompensation.

transitions.condition: The CPAP mask seal is maintained without interruption through packaging and transport, allowing continued alveolar recruitment and preload reduction.
The crew breaks the CPAP mask seal during transport (e.g., to let the patient talk or during movement) rather than maintaining continuous pressure, causing an abrupt loss of PEEP.

phases.name: CPAP seal maintained continuously
phases.description: Continuous, uninterrupted CPAP further improves oxygenation and work of breathing. The patient is packaged and transported without breaking the mask seal.
phases.triggerCondition: With the CPAP seal maintained continuously and oxygen titrated appropriately, the patient's work of breathing and oxygenation steadily improve through transport.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, CPAP mask maintained with good seal
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Markedly improved, minimal accessory muscle use
otherFindings: Rales decreased, now limited to bases only
Patient calm and tolerating CPAP well
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Gestures thumbs up, mask remains in place

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs and work of breathing after CPAP; document response to therapy
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Subsequent vital signs and physical exam to assess for change after the interventions
expectedActions.rationale: Documents therapeutic response and guides continued titration of CPAP settings.

phases.name: CPAP seal broken en route
phases.description: The crew breaks the CPAP mask seal during transport, causing an abrupt loss of positive pressure and rapid return of severe respiratory distress.
phases.triggerCondition: The crew removes or loosens the CPAP mask during transport rather than maintaining a continuous seal, per protocol causing a significant decrease in airway pressures and abrupt decompensation from atelectasis and alveolar collapse.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but distressed, mask seal disrupted
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Rapidly worsening, marked accessory muscle use returns
otherFindings: CPAP mask seal broken, positive pressure lost

expectedActions.shortAction: Immediately reapply CPAP mask and reestablish a continuous seal
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Breaking the mask seal causes a significant decrease in airway pressures and may lead to abrupt decompensation due to atelectasis and alveolar collapse.
expectedActions.rationale: Prompt reapplication of the seal is required to reverse the abrupt loss of PEEP and recruited alveoli.
